title: Design patterns and their families
idea: A design pattern is a named, proven solution shape for a recurring design problem; the Gang of Four group them into creational, structural and behavioural families.
points: Creational patterns control how objects are made, hiding which concrete class gets built.
Structural patterns compose objects: they wrap, adapt or group them behind one interface.
Behavioural patterns divide work between objects and define how those objects communicate.
A pattern name is shared vocabulary: "Strategy pattern" explains a design in two words.

Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Singleton, Builder, Prototype, Object Pool (not GoF)

Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight, Proxy

Chain of Responsibility, Command, Mediator, Observer, Strategy, Template Method, State, Visitor, Iterator, Memento

hero.caption: Classify a problem by its question first; the family narrows which pattern to reach for.

code.title: The problem
code.caption: No patterns: one format decision is made twice with switches, and the copies drift apart.

walk.text: The render decision switches on a string. A developer added the `xml` branch here.
The extension decision repeats the same switch elsewhere, and `xml` is missing.
The `default` branch hides the gap. Nothing fails; it quietly answers `txt`.
Run it: the XML body is saved as a `.txt` file. Two decisions, one forgotten.

code.title: One per family
code.caption: The same feature with one small pattern from each family. Later chapters teach each in depth.

walk.text: Behavioural: `Exporter` is a strategy. Each format owns both decisions, so neither drifts.
Each concrete exporter is a small immutable record with one job.
Creational: a simple factory maps each name to a class in one place. Not the Factory Method pattern.
An unknown format fails loudly instead of falling into a silent default.
Structural: `Titled` wraps any exporter, adding a title line without editing it.
The caller combines all three and never names a concrete exporter class.

pitfalls: Forcing a pattern onto a two-line problem; reviewers see extra classes and no gained flexibility.
Naming a class after a pattern it does not follow; readers then misjudge how it behaves.
Memorising class diagrams without the problem; in interviews you cannot say when to use one.

quiz.q: You must add retries around a PaymentClient you cannot edit. Which family?
options: Creational: it changes how the client is constructed
Behavioural: retries change how objects communicate
Structural: wrap the client behind the same interface
None: copy the client and add a loop
quiz.why: Adding behaviour by wrapping an existing object behind its own interface is composition, the structural family's job. The Decorator pattern in c07 does exactly this.

takeaway: Creational builds, structural composes, behavioural divides the work.
